newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi starts payment of some pharmaceutical debt.
newsitem.headline: Saudi starts payment of some pharmaceutical debt.

text.p: Saudi Arabia, one of the Middle East's top pharmaceutical consumers, has started paying part of hundreds of millions of dollars in arrears to international suppliers, industry sources and bankers said on Monday.
They said the payments to suppliers mostly from Europe and the United States started in the last week of August.
"We are encouraged...The process of repaying has started slowly but definitely," one source at an international company said from his office in Saudi Arabia.
Some of the biggest European and U.S. companies had been pressing the Saudi government and the health and finance ministries to settle the arrears, some going back to 1993.
Industry sources put the arrears at close to $1 billion.
But Kevin Taecker, chief economist at the Saudi American Bank said in his economic outlook for September total arrears to medical suppliers and contractors stood at $2 billion to $3 billion.

He said the Saudi cabinet had recently "resolved to pay some $2 billion to $3 billion in amounts owed to medical suppliers and contractors at a rate of 20 percent per year over five years in cash, but without a promissory note."
The pharmaceutical executive confirmed that bigger suppliers would be paid over five years, but it was not clear when these payments would start.

Experts say Saudi Arabia is one of the Middle East's largest consumers of pharmaceutical products with the size of the market valued at more than three billion riyals ($800 million) annually of which local production accounts for less than 15 percent.

Saudi officials have been encouraging private investment in the industry to offset the huge drug import bill. Saudi Arabia has at least two producing projects and five being planned for production in the next three yeras.
The industry sources and bankers said the government was meeting payments for 1996 contracts on time.
The official Saudi Press Agency on Sunday said Health Minister Osama bin Abdul-Majid Shobokshi signed 156 deals worth 666 million riyals for the import of pharmaceutical products.
The industry sources said the 666 million riyals represented payments for pharmaceutical products delivered by suppliers under contracts in 1996.
"For the first time in many years payment is being made on time," one said.

In 1995 Riyadh began issuing special bonds to make a dent in the estimated $5 billion outstanding to contractors. It has also issued special certificates to farmers estimated to be worth nine billion riyals.
Taecker said in his study the finance ministry settled up to $6 billion of the arrears in cash, bonds and special payment certificates since March 1995 to contractors and farmers.
The debt had been mounting since the early 1990s as a result of huge Gulf War liabilities amid soft world oil prices.
